goals: Explain why organisms reproduce and distinguish asexual from sexual reproduction
Describe fission, budding, fragmentation, regeneration, spore formation and vegetative propagation with examples
Name the parts of a flower and describe pollination and fertilisation
Explain how the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit

slides.heading: Reproduction
slides.body_md: Part 1: how living things make more of their own kind, from a single dividing cell to a flowering tree.

rows: a little different from each parent

visual.alt: Table comparing asexual and sexual reproduction by parents, offspring and example

slides.narration: Every kind of living thing makes more of its own kind. This is called reproduction. Some organisms do it alone, by splitting or growing a new part. Others need two parents. In this part we look at both ways, and then follow a flower from pollination to seed and fruit.

slides.heading: Why do organisms reproduce?
slides.body_md: **Reproduction** is the making of new individuals of the same kind. It keeps a species going after individuals die. There are two main modes. In **asexual reproduction** a **single parent** makes offspring that are **identical** to it, without gametes. In **sexual reproduction** two special cells, the **male gamete** and the **female gamete**, fuse to make a **zygote** that grows into a new individual. Offspring then show **variation**.

rows: differ from each other and from parents

visual.alt: Table comparing asexual and sexual reproduction by parents, gametes, offspring and speed

slides.narration: Reproduction keeps a species going after individuals die. In asexual reproduction, one parent makes offspring that are identical to it, and no gametes are needed. In sexual reproduction, a male gamete and a female gamete fuse to make a zygote, which grows into a new individual. These offspring show variation, so they are not exactly like their parents.

slides.heading: Fission and budding
slides.body_md: In **binary fission** one cell divides into **two** daughter cells, as in *Amoeba*. In **multiple fission** the nucleus divides many times and the cell breaks into **many** daughter cells, as in *Plasmodium*, the malaria parasite. In **budding** a small outgrowth, the **bud**, forms on the parent, grows and separates; **yeast** reproduces this way, which is why dough and idli batter rise.

slides.narration: Look at the three rows. In binary fission, an Amoeba divides its nucleus and then its body into two daughter cells. In multiple fission, the nucleus of Plasmodium divides again and again and the cell breaks into many daughter cells. In budding, a yeast cell forms a small bud, which grows and then separates from the parent.

slides.heading: Fragmentation, regeneration and spores
slides.body_md: ***Hydra*** also reproduces by **budding**, but its bud grows into a small Hydra. In **fragmentation**, the body of *Spirogyra*, a green alga with a thread-like body, breaks into pieces and each piece grows into a new filament. In **regeneration**, a flatworm such as *Planaria* that is cut into pieces regrows the missing parts, so each piece can become a whole worm. In **spore formation**, *Rhizopus* (bread mould) makes tiny spores in round **sporangia**; spores float in air and grow on damp food.

slides.heading: Vegetative propagation
slides.body_md: In **vegetative propagation** a new plant grows from a **vegetative part** of the parent: a root, stem or leaf. A potato tuber sprouts from its **eyes**; a *Bryophyllum* leaf grows **plantlets** at its notches; a **rose cutting** with a node makes roots in soil. In **grafting** a cut shoot, the **scion**, is joined to a rooted plant, the **stock**. Gardeners use these methods to keep a good variety and to grow plants that rarely make seeds.

slides.heading: Worked example: which method is it?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the mode of reproduction in each case: (a) a dosa batter froths because of cells with small outgrowths; (b) a leaf dropped in damp soil grows tiny plants at its edge; (c) a pond thread breaks in a storm and each piece grows; (d) a cell splits equally into two.

**Step 1.** Look for the clue word in each case: outgrowth, leaf, break, split.

**Step 2.** (a) **budding** in yeast; (b) **vegetative propagation** (leaf of Bryophyllum); (c) **fragmentation** (Spirogyra); (d) **binary fission**.

visual.alt: Table of four cases with the clue and the mode of reproduction

slides.narration: To name a method, look for the clue. A dosa batter that froths has yeast cells with small outgrowths, which is budding. A leaf that grows tiny plants at its edge shows vegetative propagation. A pond thread that breaks, with each piece growing, is fragmentation. A cell that splits equally into two is binary fission.

slides.heading: Sexual reproduction
slides.body_md: In sexual reproduction two **gametes** fuse in **fertilisation** to form a **zygote**, which develops into an **embryo**. A **male gamete** is small and moves; a **female gamete**, the **egg**, is large and holds food. Because the offspring get material from both parents, they show **variation**, which helps a species when conditions change. Sexual reproduction is slower and needs more energy than asexual reproduction.

the young organism that grows from the zygote

visual.alt: Table of four terms of sexual reproduction with their meaning

slides.narration: In sexual reproduction, two gametes fuse in fertilisation to make a zygote, which grows into an embryo. The male gamete is small and can move. The female gamete, the egg, is large and holds food. The offspring get material from both parents, so they show variation. This helps a species when its surroundings change.

slides.heading: Parts of a flower
slides.body_md: The flower is the **reproductive part** of a flowering plant. **Sepals** protect the bud and **petals** attract insects. The **stamen** is the **male** part: an **anther** that makes **pollen grains** on a **filament**. The **pistil** (carpel) is the **female** part: **stigma** (sticky top), **style** and **ovary**, which holds **ovules**, each with an egg cell. A flower with both stamens and pistil is **bisexual**, as in hibiscus; a flower with only one is **unisexual**, as in papaya.

slides.narration: The flower is the reproductive part of a plant. Sepals protect the bud and petals attract insects. The stamen is the male part, with an anther that makes pollen grains on a filament. The pistil is the female part, with a sticky stigma, a style and an ovary that holds the ovules. A flower with both parts is bisexual, like hibiscus. One with only one kind is unisexual, like papaya.

slides.heading: Pollination
slides.body_md: **Pollination** is the transfer of pollen from an **anther** to a **stigma**. In **self-pollination** the pollen reaches a stigma of the **same flower** (or another flower of the same plant). In **cross-pollination** it reaches a flower of **another plant** of the same kind, which gives more variation. **Agents** carry the pollen: insects, wind, water, birds or bats.

slides.narration: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. In self pollination, the pollen reaches a stigma of the same flower, or of another flower on the same plant. In cross pollination, it reaches a flower of another plant of the same kind. Insects, wind, water, birds and bats carry the pollen. Bright, scented flowers attract insects, while wind pollinated flowers have light, dry pollen.

slides.heading: Worked example: ovules to seeds
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A chilli ovary has 36 ovules. If 75 % of them are fertilised, how many seeds will the chilli have?

**Step 1.** Each **fertilised ovule** becomes **one seed**.

**Step 2.** Seeds $= \dfrac{75}{100} \times 36 = 27$.

The remaining 9 ovules are not fertilised and do not form seeds.

rows: Ovules that do not form seeds

visual.alt: Table of ovules, fraction fertilised, seeds formed and ovules without seeds

slides.narration: A chilli ovary has thirty six ovules, and seventy five percent are fertilised. Each fertilised ovule becomes one seed. Seventy five hundredths of thirty six is twenty seven. So the chilli has twenty seven seeds, and the other nine ovules do not form seeds.

slides.heading: After fertilisation: seed and fruit
slides.body_md: After fertilisation the **ovule** becomes the **seed**, with the embryo inside. The **ovary** grows and becomes the **fruit**, and the ovary wall becomes the fruit wall. Petals and sepals usually dry up and fall. Fruit protects the seeds and often helps them spread.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Asexual reproduction: one parent, identical offspring; fission, budding, fragmentation, regeneration, spores, vegetative propagation.
Sexual reproduction: fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote; offspring show variation.
Flower: sepal, petal, stamen (anther, filament), pistil (stigma, style, ovary with ovules).
Pollination moves pollen from anther to stigma; self or cross, by insects, wind, water, birds or bats.
Fertilisation: pollen tube carries the male gamete to the egg; ovule becomes seed, ovary becomes fruit.

visual.alt: Table of flower parts before fertilisation and what they become

slides.narration: To sum up. Asexual reproduction needs one parent and gives identical offspring. Sexual reproduction joins a male and a female gamete. A flower has sepals, petals, stamens and a pistil. Pollen moves from anther to stigma by pollination. After fertilisation the zygote becomes the embryo, the ovule becomes the seed, and the ovary becomes the fruit.

slides.heading: Gametes and fertilisation in humans
slides.body_md: The male gamete is the **sperm**, a tiny cell with a tail so it can swim. The female gamete is the **egg** (ovum), a much larger round cell. Humans have **internal fertilisation**: a sperm meets the egg **inside the female body**. The zygote then divides and the embryo settles in the **uterus**, where it grows for about nine months.

slides.narration: The male gamete is the sperm. It is tiny and has a tail for swimming. The female gamete is the egg, which is much larger and round. In humans, fertilisation is internal, which means that a sperm meets the egg inside the female body. The zygote divides, and the embryo settles in the uterus, where it grows for about nine months.

slides.heading: The male reproductive system
slides.body_md: This is a simple labelled outline. The **testes** make sperms and the hormone testosterone. They hang in the **scrotum**, which keeps them slightly cooler than the rest of the body. Each testis is joined to an **epididymis** where sperms are stored, and a **vas deferens**, a tube that carries sperms up. The **seminal vesicles** and the **prostate gland** add fluids; together with the sperms they form **semen**. The **urethra** carries semen, and also urine, out through the **penis**.

slides.heading: Female organs and their functions

slides.narration: In the female body, the ovary makes eggs and female hormones. About one egg is released each month. The fallopian tube picks up the egg, and fertilisation usually takes place there. The uterus is where the embryo settles and grows. The cervix is the narrow lower end of the uterus, and the vagina is the passage that connects it to the outside.

slides.heading: Worked example: following an egg
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Trace the path of an egg that is fertilised, and say where each stage happens.

**Step 1.** The egg is released from an **ovary** and enters the **fallopian tube**.

**Step 2.** A sperm fuses with it in the tube: **fertilisation**, forming a **zygote**.

**Step 3.** The zygote divides as it moves to the **uterus**, where the embryo settles in the soft lining and grows.

rows: on its way down the tube

slides.narration: Let us follow an egg. It is released from an ovary and enters the fallopian tube. If a sperm meets it there, they fuse, which is fertilisation, and a zygote forms. The zygote divides as it moves towards the uterus. There the embryo settles in the soft lining of the uterus and grows.

slides.heading: Adolescence and puberty
slides.body_md: **Adolescence** is the stage between childhood and adulthood, from about age 10 to 19. **Puberty**, when the body becomes able to reproduce, usually starts between about 10 and 14, earlier in some people and later in others, and **both are normal**. Changes are caused by **hormones**, chemical messengers in the blood. They affect the body, and also feelings and thoughts.

slides.narration: Adolescence is the stage between childhood and adulthood, from about age ten to nineteen. Puberty usually starts between about ten and fourteen, earlier in some people and later in others, and both are normal. Hormones cause the changes. Girls develop breasts and have periods. Boys get a deeper voice and facial hair. Both have a growth spurt and may get pimples.

slides.heading: The menstrual cycle
slides.body_md: In girls, the lining of the uterus thickens each month to prepare for an embryo. If no egg is fertilised, the lining and a little blood leave through the vagina. This is **menstruation**, or a **period**. It is a **natural**, healthy process. It lasts about **3 to 7 days**, and a cycle is often around 28 days (it can be 21 to 35 days). In the first years the cycle may be **irregular**.

slides.narration: In girls, the lining of the uterus thickens each month. If no egg is fertilised, the lining and a little blood leave through the vagina. This is menstruation, or a period. It is natural and healthy. It lasts about three to seven days, and a cycle is often about twenty eight days, though it can be from twenty one to thirty five. In the first years, cycles may be irregular.

slides.heading: Worked example: marking the calendar
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Meena notes 5 June as the first day of her period. Her cycle is 30 days. When should she expect the next period to start?

**Step 1.** Add the cycle length: $5 + 30 = 35$.

**Step 2.** June has 30 days, so subtract 30 and move to July: $35 - 30 = 5$.

The next period is expected around **5 July**. Because cycles can vary by a few days, this is only an estimate.

The next period is expected around the fifth of July. Since cycles can vary by a few days, this is only an estimate, and keeping a calendar helps.

slides.heading: Menstrual hygiene
slides.body_md: Periods are not dirty or shameful. Good habits prevent infection and discomfort. Use a clean **pad**, **cloth that is washed and dried in sunlight**, or other safe product, and **change it every 4 to 6 hours**. Wash hands before and after changing. Wrap used pads and throw them in a dustbin, never down the toilet. Bathe daily and wear clean undergarments. Have **school and home toilets** with water, privacy and a bin.

slides.heading: Looking after your body
slides.body_md: Hormones make the body grow fast, so it needs good care. Eat **balanced meals** with dal, milk, eggs or pulses, green leafy vegetables, fruit and whole grains. **Iron-rich foods**, such as spinach, jaggery and dal, are important for girls because of monthly blood loss. Drink clean water, **sleep 8 to 9 hours**, play or exercise every day, and wash your face and body daily because oily skin can cause pimples. Avoid **tobacco and other drugs**.

Iron rich foods such as spinach and jaggery are important, especially for girls. Drink clean water, sleep eight to nine hours, and play or exercise every day. Wash your face and body daily. Stay away from tobacco and other drugs.

slides.body_md: Many wrong ideas are passed around. Correct facts help you feel confident.

slides.narration: Let us look at some myths. Some people say a period makes a girl impure. A period is a normal body process, and nothing about it is impure. Some think girls should not bathe or exercise during periods, but light exercise and daily baths are healthy. A cracking voice in a boy is normal. Pimples come from hormones and oily skin. slides.heading: Whom to ask, and staying safe
slides.body_md: It is normal to have questions. Ask a **parent, elder, teacher, school counsellor, doctor** or a trained health worker, and use reliable books. See a doctor if a period is very painful, very heavy, or stops for months after it was regular, or if you feel very low or worried. **Your body belongs to you.** If anyone makes you feel uncomfortable or touches you in a way you do not like, say no, move away and tell a trusted adult at once.

sections.heading: 1. Reproduction and the two modes
sections.body_md:
**Reproduction** makes new individuals of the same kind and keeps a species going. In **asexual reproduction** one parent produces identical offspring (clones) without gametes. In **sexual reproduction** a male and a female gamete fuse to form a zygote, and the offspring show variation.

**Fission:** *Amoeba* divides into two (binary fission); *Plasmodium* divides into many (multiple fission). **Budding:** a bud grows on the parent and separates, as in yeast.

key_terms.definition_md: Reproduction from a single parent, with no gametes, giving identical offspring.
Division of one cell into two daughter cells.
Division of one cell into many daughter cells.
Formation of a small outgrowth that grows and separates from the parent.

sections.heading: 2. Fragmentation, regeneration, spores and vegetative propagation
sections.body_md:
**Fragmentation:** the body of *Spirogyra* breaks into pieces and each grows into a filament. **Regeneration:** a cut *Planaria* regrows missing parts, so each piece can become a worm. **Spores:** *Rhizopus* makes spores in sporangia that grow on damp food. *Hydra* also reproduces by budding.

**Vegetative propagation:** a new plant grows from a root, stem or leaf: potato eyes, *Bryophyllum* leaf plantlets, rose cuttings. **Grafting** joins a scion to a stock. Advantages: fast, keeps a good variety, works for plants that make few seeds. Limit: little variation.

key_terms.definition_md: Breaking of a body into pieces that each grow into a new organism.
Regrowth of missing body parts from a piece of the organism.
A tiny cell, produced in large numbers, that can grow into a new organism.
Growth of a new plant from a vegetative part of the parent.
A cut shoot (scion) joined to a rooted plant (stock).

sections.heading: 3. Sexual reproduction and the flower
sections.body_md: Two gametes fuse in **fertilisation** to give a **zygote**, which grows into an **embryo**. The flower is the reproductive part of a plant. **Stamen** (male): anther on a filament makes pollen grains. **Pistil** (female): stigma, style, and ovary holding ovules, each with an egg cell. Sepals protect the bud, petals attract insects. A flower with both stamens and pistil is bisexual (hibiscus); with one only it is unisexual (papaya).

key_terms.definition_md: A male or female sex cell.
The cell formed when a male gamete fuses with an egg.
The part of the stamen that makes pollen grains.
The sticky top of the pistil that receives pollen.
A structure in the ovary that holds an egg cell.

sections.heading: 4. Pollination, fertilisation, seed and fruit
sections.body_md:
**Pollination** is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. **Self-pollination** is within a flower (or between flowers of one plant); **cross-pollination** is between flowers of different plants and gives more variation. Agents: insects, wind, water, birds, bats.

After landing, the pollen grain grows a **pollen tube** through the style to the ovule. The male gamete fuses with the egg: **fertilisation**. Then the zygote becomes the embryo, the **ovule becomes the seed**, the **ovary becomes the fruit**, and petals and sepals usually dry up.

key_terms.definition_md: Transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma.
Transfer of pollen to a flower of another plant of the same kind.
A tube grown by a pollen grain that carries the male gamete to the ovule.
The ripened ovary, which holds and protects the seeds.

sections.heading: 5. Human reproductive systems
sections.body_md:
**Male:** testes (make sperms and testosterone) lie in the scrotum; epididymis stores sperms; vas deferens carries them; seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids (semen); urethra and penis pass semen out.

**Female:** ovaries make eggs and female hormones; fallopian tubes carry the egg and are the usual site of fertilisation; the uterus holds the growing embryo; the cervix is its narrow end; the vagina is the passage to the outside. Fertilisation is internal; the embryo grows in the uterus for about nine months.

sections.heading: 6. Adolescence and reproductive health
sections.body_md:
**Adolescence** (about 10 to 19 years) includes **puberty**, driven by hormones. Girls: breasts develop, periods begin. Boys: deeper voice, facial hair. Both: growth spurt, body hair, pimples, strong feelings. Timing differs and all of it is normal.

**Menstruation** is the natural monthly shedding of the uterine lining (3 to 7 days; cycle often about 28 days, 21 to 35 normal; irregular at first). **Hygiene:** clean pad or sun-dried cloth, change every 4 to 6 hours, wash hands, dispose safely, bathe daily. **Health:** balanced food with iron, 8 to 9 hours of sleep, exercise, no tobacco or drugs. Ask a trusted adult, teacher or doctor; see a doctor for very painful or heavy periods.

questions.stem_md: Under a microscope, a student sees a baker's yeast cell with a small round swelling on its side, smaller than the cell itself. This is most likely:

options.text_md: binary fission, because the two parts are equal
fertilisation, because two cells have fused
regeneration after the cell was cut
budding, a form of asexual reproduction

questions.solution_md: A small outgrowth that is smaller than the parent is a bud, so the yeast is reproducing by budding — option (d). Binary fission gives two equal parts.

questions.stem_md: A malaria parasite inside a red blood cell divides its nucleus several times and then breaks into many small cells. This is:

options.text_md: multiple fission, which gives many daughter cells
binary fission, which gives two daughter cells
budding, which gives a small outgrowth
fragmentation, which needs a thread-like body

questions.solution_md: Repeated nuclear division followed by break-up into many cells is multiple fission — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A farmer cuts a seed potato into four pieces, each with a bud (eye), and plants all four. The four plants will be:

options.text_md: nearly identical to each other and to the parent plant
quite different from one another, like children of two parents
weaker, because no gametes were used
unable to make tubers of their own

questions.solution_md: This is vegetative propagation from one parent, with no gametes, so the plants are clones of the parent and of each other — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Spores of a mould can spread over a wide area and are made in very large numbers. Which feature of spores explains how this helps the mould?

options.text_md: Each spore is a large cell with stored food
They are tiny and light, so air carries them and some will land on food
Each spore is produced after two parents fuse
Spores only form when the mould is cut into pieces

questions.solution_md: Tiny, light spores float in air, and since there are so many, some reach damp food and grow — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a rubber plantation in Kerala, a bud from a high-yielding tree is fixed on a young rooted plant of another tree. This method is called:

options.text_md: grafting, a kind of vegetative propagation

questions.solution_md: Joining a cut part (the scion) to a rooted plant (the stock) is grafting — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Plants grown from the eyes of one potato are almost identical to the parent.

**Reason (R):** Vegetative propagation does not involve the fusion of gametes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is true, and it explains A: with no gametes and no mixing of material from two parents, the offspring are copies — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Yeast reproduces by binary fission, producing two equal cells.
questions.solution_md: False. Yeast reproduces by budding: a small bud grows on the parent and separates.

questions.stem_md: In bread mould, the round sporangia release tiny cells called ___ that grow on damp food.
questions.solution_md: Sporangia release **spores**.

questions.stem_md: Match each organism or plant (Column A) with the method by which it reproduces asexually (Column B).

options.text_md: A green thread in a pond that breaks into pieces
A flatworm cut in two that regrows
A small outgrowth on the body wall of Hydra
A leaf of Bryophyllum with plantlets at its notches

questions.solution_md: Spirogyra threads fragment, a cut flatworm regenerates, Hydra forms buds, and Bryophyllum leaves make plantlets (vegetative propagation).

questions.stem_md: A spoonful of yeast is added to sugar solution in a warm place, and after a few hours the liquid is cloudy with many more yeast cells. Explain how the number of cells increased.

answer.model_answer_md: Yeast reproduces by budding. A small bud forms on a parent cell, grows, receives a nucleus and separates as a new cell. In warm sugar solution this happens quickly in many cells at once, so the number of cells rises fast.

questions.solution_md: Budding: bud forms, grows and separates; fast in warm sugar solution.

marking_scheme.step: Yeast reproduces by budding: a bud grows and separates
Many cells bud quickly in warm, sugary conditions

questions.stem_md: State three differences between asexual and sexual reproduction.

answer.model_answer_md: Asexual reproduction needs only one parent, while sexual reproduction usually involves two. Asexual reproduction forms no gametes, but sexual reproduction depends on the fusion of a male and a female gamete. The offspring of asexual reproduction are identical to the parent, whereas sexual offspring show variation and differ from both parents.

questions.solution_md: One parent versus two; no gametes versus gametes; identical versus varied offspring.

questions.stem_md: Give three advantages of growing new plants by vegetative propagation, with an example of a plant grown in this way.

answer.model_answer_md: Vegetative propagation is faster than growing from seed, so a gardener gets flowering or fruiting plants sooner. It keeps all the good qualities of the parent, because the new plants are identical to it. It also works for plants that rarely make seeds, such as the rose, which is grown from stem cuttings, and Bryophyllum, grown from its leaf plantlets.

questions.solution_md: Faster; keeps qualities of parent; works for seedless plants; rose cutting.

marking_scheme.step: Keeps good qualities because plants are identical
Works for plants without seeds, with an example

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is asexual reproduction?

(b) Describe, with simple labelled sketches, binary fission in Amoeba and budding in yeast.

(c) Name one organism that reproduces by fragmentation and say how.

answer.model_answer_md: Asexual reproduction is reproduction by a single parent without gametes, so offspring are identical to it. In Amoeba the nucleus lengthens and divides, the cell pinches in the middle, and two daughter cells form. In yeast a small bud appears on the parent cell, grows and receives a nucleus, then separates as a new cell. Spirogyra reproduces by fragmentation: its thread-like body breaks into pieces and each piece grows into a new filament.

questions.solution_md: Definition; Amoeba fission steps; yeast budding steps; Spirogyra fragmentation.

marking_scheme.step: (a) One parent, no gametes, identical offspring

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A school science club keeps one Hydra in an aquarium and counts it every third day. The counts are given for practice.

| Day | Full-grown Hydra | Buds attached |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 |
| 6 | 1 | 2 |
| 9 | 3 | 0 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Budding

**(b)** $3 - 1 = 2$ new Hydra.

**(c)** (i) They come from one parent by budding, without the fusion of gametes, so they receive the same material as the parent and are clones of it.

**OR** (ii) Only one parent was present in the aquarium at the start, and the new Hydra appeared as buds on its body. No male and female gametes were involved, so it is asexual reproduction.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Buds appear on the parent, grow, and separate as new Hydra by day 9 — option (a).

**(b)** New Hydra = 3 − 1 = 2.

**(c)** (i) One parent, no gametes, so identical.

(ii) Single parent; buds on its body; no gametes.

children.solution_md: Buds appear on the parent, grow, and separate as new Hydra by day 9 — option (a).

children.stem_md: How many new Hydra were formed by day 9?

answer.model_answer_md: $3 - 1 = 2$ new Hydra.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Why are the new Hydra almost identical to the parent?

answer.model_answer_md: They come from one parent by budding, without the fusion of gametes, so they receive the same material as the parent and are clones of it.

answer.model_answer_md: Only one parent was present in the aquarium at the start, and the new Hydra appeared as buds on its body. No male and female gametes were involved, so it is asexual reproduction.

questions.stem_md: In a hibiscus flower, which part produces the pollen grains?
questions.solution_md: The anther at the top of the filament makes pollen grains — option (a). The stigma receives pollen, and the ovule holds the egg cell.

questions.stem_md: After fertilisation in a guava flower, the part that grows and ripens into the fruit is the:
questions.solution_md: The ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules in it become seeds — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A bee lands on a mustard flower and pollen sticks to the top of the pistil, which is rough and sticky. This part is the:
questions.solution_md: The sticky top of the pistil, which receives pollen, is the stigma — option (d).

questions.stem_md:

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

**Assertion (A):** Seeds formed by cross-pollination give plants that are all identical to the parent plant.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Wind-pollinated plants, such as maize, make very large amounts of pollen.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Pollination and fertilisation mean the same thing in a flowering plant.
questions.solution_md: False. Pollination is the transfer of pollen to a stigma; fertilisation is the later fusion of the male gamete with the egg.

questions.stem_md: The ovary of a flower has 40 ovules, and 60 % of them are fertilised. How many seeds will the fruit have?

questions.stem_md: Why do farmers sometimes plant different varieties of a crop in neighbouring rows to encourage cross-pollination?

answer.model_answer_md: Cross-pollination brings together pollen and egg cells from two different plants. The seeds that form combine material from both parents, so the offspring show more variation, and some may be stronger or better able to survive disease and changes in climate.

answer.model_answer_md: The diagram should show the sepal, petal, stamen with anther and filament, and the pistil with stigma, style, ovary and ovules. The anther makes pollen grains, the stigma receives the pollen, and the ovule contains the egg cell and becomes a seed after fertilisation. questions.stem_md:
(a) What is pollination? Name two agents of pollination.

(b) Describe the steps from the landing of a pollen grain to the formation of the zygote.

(c) State what the ovule and the ovary become after fertilisation.

answer.model_answer_md: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma, and insects or wind can carry the pollen. On the stigma the pollen grain grows a pollen tube down through the style to an ovule. The male gamete moves along the tube and fuses with the egg cell, and this fertilisation forms the zygote, which divides to form the embryo. After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

(c) Ovule to seed, ovary to fruit

he is growing up in the wrong way
